bio_edx.2.0.summary: Organisms can reproduce asexually (one parent, mitosis, genetically identical offspring) or sexually (two parents, gametes made by meiosis, fertilisation, genetically different offspring). Asexual reproduction needs no mate and has a rapid reproductive cycle, but gives no variation in the population. Sexual reproduction gives variation in the population, which helps a species survive change, but it requires finding a mate, which costs time and energy. This is separate-science (triple) Biology content only.

core.h: What this spec point asks for (Biology only)
core.p: Spec points 3.1B and 3.2B are in **bold with a B**, which means they are examined only in separate-science GCSE Biology (triple), not in Combined Science. You must be able to **explain** (not just list) some advantages and disadvantages of each type of reproduction.
bullets: **3.1B Asexual reproduction**: advantages include the **lack of need to find a mate** and a **rapid reproductive cycle**; the disadvantage is **no variation in the population**.
**3.2B Sexual reproduction**: the advantage is **variation in the population**; the disadvantage is **the requirement of finding a mate**.
The command word is **explain**, so every point needs a reason or a consequence: say what the feature is AND why it helps or harms the organism or the population.
Notice the two lists mirror each other: each advantage of one type is the disadvantage of the other.

callouts.p: Asexual: no need to find a mate, rapid reproductive cycle, but no variation in the population. Sexual: variation in the population, but requires finding a mate.

core.p: In asexual reproduction there is only **one parent**. The offspring are produced by **mitosis**, so no gametes are made and there is no fertilisation. Because mitosis copies the chromosomes exactly, all the offspring are **genetically identical** to the parent and to each other. They are **clones**.
bullets: One parent only, so no mate is needed.
Cells divide by **mitosis**: each new cell receives an exact copy of every chromosome.
No gametes and no fertilisation, so there is no mixing of genetic information from two individuals.
Offspring are genetically identical (clones). The only source of genetic difference is a rare **mutation**.
Examples: bacteria dividing in two, strawberry plants growing runners, potato plants forming tubers, daffodils forming bulbs.

callouts.p: Reproduction involving only one parent, with no fusion of gametes, producing genetically identical offspring (clones) by mitosis.

core.p: Sexual reproduction involves **two parents**. Each parent makes **gametes** (sex cells) by **meiosis**. Gametes are **haploid**: they have half the normal number of chromosomes. At **fertilisation** a male gamete fuses with a female gamete to form a **diploid zygote**, which has genetic information from both parents.
bullets: Two parents are needed, so the organism must usually find a mate (or, in plants, be pollinated).
Gametes in animals are sperm and egg cells; in flowering plants they are in the pollen and the ovule.
Meiosis produces gametes that are genetically different from each other.
Fertilisation is random: any male gamete can fuse with any female gamete.
Each offspring inherits a different mixture of alleles, so offspring are **genetically different** from their parents and from each other. This is **variation**.

callouts.p: Reproduction involving the fusion of a male gamete and a female gamete (fertilisation) from two parents, producing offspring that are genetically different from each other and from the parents.

core.h: Advantage of asexual reproduction 1: no need to find a mate
core.p: Because only one parent is involved, an organism can reproduce **on its own**. It does not have to spend time and energy searching for, attracting or competing for a mate.
bullets: **Time and energy are saved**, and can be used for growth or for producing more offspring instead.
A **single isolated individual** can start a whole new population. One bacterium landing on food, or one plant arriving in a new habitat, is enough to colonise it.
Reproduction is not prevented when the population is small or spread out and mates are hard to find.
Plants do not need to rely on pollinators such as insects or on wind to carry pollen.

callouts.p: Do not stop at 'no mate is needed'. Add the consequence: so less time and energy is used, or so a single organism can colonise a new area.

core.h: Advantage of asexual reproduction 2: rapid reproductive cycle
core.p: Asexual reproduction is **fast**. There is no need to make gametes, find a mate, or wait for fertilisation, so many offspring can be produced in a short time.
bullets: Large numbers of offspring are produced quickly, so the **population increases rapidly**.
The organism can **take advantage of favourable conditions** (plenty of food, water, space, warmth) before they change or before competitors arrive.
Example: some bacteria can divide about every 20 minutes when conditions are ideal, so one cell can become thousands within a few hours.
If the parent is well suited to its environment, all its offspring inherit exactly the same alleles, so they are **equally well suited** as long as the environment stays the same.

callouts.p: Fast reproduction lets a population quickly use up available resources and colonise a habitat, out-competing slower-reproducing organisms.

core.h: Disadvantage of asexual reproduction: no variation in the population
core.p: All the offspring are genetically identical, so there is **no (genetic) variation in the population**. This is fine while the environment is stable, but it is dangerous when the environment changes.
bullets: If the environment changes (a new disease, a new predator, a change in climate, less food), every individual is affected in the **same way**.
If one individual is **susceptible to a disease**, they all are, so the disease could kill the **whole population**.
There are no individuals with different alleles that might allow them to survive, so the population is **less likely to adapt** and may die out.
With almost no variation, **natural selection** has nothing to act on, so the species cannot evolve quickly in response to change.
Offspring often grow close to the parent (for example strawberry runners), so there can be **competition** for light, water and mineral ions.

callouts.t: Identical is not the same as weak
callouts.p: Clones are not less healthy in themselves. The problem is at population level: because all are identical, one change in the environment could affect all of them.

core.h: Advantage of sexual reproduction: variation in the population
core.p: Sexual reproduction mixes genetic information from two parents, so the offspring show **genetic variation**. Variation makes it more likely that the population survives when the environment changes.
bullets: Individuals have **different combinations of alleles**, so they have different characteristics.
If the environment changes, **some individuals are likely to have characteristics that let them survive** the new conditions (for example resistance to a new disease).
The survivors reproduce and pass on the advantageous alleles to their offspring. This is **natural selection**.
Over many generations the population becomes **better adapted** to the new conditions, so the species is less likely to become extinct.
So variation gives a **survival advantage to the population** (not necessarily to every individual).

callouts.p: Variation -> some individuals better adapted to a change -> they survive and reproduce -> advantageous alleles passed on -> population survives.

core.h: Disadvantage of sexual reproduction: the requirement of finding a mate
core.p: Two parents are needed, so an organism must **find a mate** before it can reproduce. This has real costs.
bullets: Finding, attracting and competing for a mate takes **time and energy**, for example in courtship displays or fighting rivals. Flowering plants use energy and materials making flowers, nectar and large amounts of pollen.
An **isolated individual cannot reproduce**: if no mate can be found, no offspring are produced.
Reproduction is **slower**, so fewer offspring are usually produced in a given time and the population grows more slowly.
Searching for or displaying to a mate can make an animal more visible to predators.
Because alleles are mixed, a well-adapted parent is not guaranteed to produce equally well-adapted offspring.

callouts.p: Write 'a mate must be found, which takes time and energy' rather than a vague phrase such as 'it is harder'.

bullets: Each row shows how one type gains where the other loses.
In an exam comparison, make a statement about **both** types in each point.

core.h: Which is better? It depends on the environment
core.p: Neither method is always best. Top answers link the method to the conditions the organism lives in.
bullets: In a **stable, favourable environment**, asexual reproduction is an advantage: the parent is already well adapted, so identical offspring will be too, and numbers rise quickly.
In a **changing environment** (new disease, changing climate), sexual reproduction is an advantage because variation means some individuals are likely to survive.
Some organisms can use **both** methods. A strawberry plant spreads quickly using runners (asexual) and also makes flowers and seeds (sexual), gaining variation and wider dispersal.
Using both gives rapid colonisation when conditions are good and variation as an insurance against change.

callouts.p: Give advantages AND disadvantages of both types, each with a reason, and link to the context in the question (for example a crop disease or a new habitat).

core.h: Applying the ideas to unfamiliar examples
core.p: Exam questions usually describe a real organism and ask you to explain why its method of reproduction is an advantage or a disadvantage. Apply the same four ideas each time.
bullets: **Crop plants grown from cuttings or tubers** (for example potatoes): all are clones, so one disease could destroy the whole crop.
**Bacteria on food or in the body**: no mate needed and a rapid reproductive cycle, so numbers increase very quickly.
**An animal species with few individuals left**: mates are hard to find, so sexual reproduction may fail and numbers fall further.
**A plant colonising bare ground**: asexual reproduction lets one plant cover the area quickly.
Always state whether offspring are genetically identical or genetically different, then give the consequence.

callouts.p: Write 'genetically identical' or 'genetically different'. Offspring of asexual reproduction can still look different because of the environment (for example less light or fewer mineral ions).

analogy.t: Photocopying versus shuffling two packs of cards
analogy.p: Asexual reproduction is like a **photocopier**: one original, no partner needed, and many copies made very quickly. But every copy has exactly the same content, so if the original has a weakness, every copy has it too. Sexual reproduction is like two people each shuffling their own pack, each giving half of their cards, and combining them into a new pack: you have to find a second person first and it takes longer, but every new pack is different, so some packs will hold a winning hand whatever game is played next. Where it breaks down: a photocopy is a lower-quality version of the original, whereas clones are fully healthy organisms, and photocopies never change, whereas rare mutations can produce small differences in clones.

terms.d: Reproduction with one parent and no fusion of gametes, producing genetically identical offspring by mitosis.
Reproduction in which a male and a female gamete from two parents fuse at fertilisation, producing genetically different offspring.
An organism that is genetically identical to its parent and to other offspring of that parent.
Cell division that produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells; the basis of asexual reproduction.
Cell division that produces four genetically different haploid gametes.
A haploid sex cell, such as a sperm cell, an egg cell or the male gamete in a pollen grain.
The fusion of a male gamete with a female gamete to form a diploid zygote.
The diploid cell formed when two gametes fuse at fertilisation.
Having one set of chromosomes (half the normal number), as in gametes.
Having two sets of chromosomes, one set from each parent, as in body cells.
Differences between individuals of the same species; genetic variation is caused by differences in alleles.
Having exactly the same alleles; true of offspring produced by asexual reproduction.
The time taken for an organism to produce a new generation of offspring; it is rapid in asexual reproduction.
A partner of the same species needed for sexual reproduction.
The process in which individuals with advantageous characteristics are more likely to survive, reproduce and pass on their alleles.
A rare, random change in DNA; the only source of genetic variation in asexually reproducing populations.

mistakes.w: Asexual reproduction is quicker.
mistakes.r: Explain it: there is a rapid reproductive cycle because no mate has to be found and no gametes are needed, so many offspring are produced in a short time and the population increases rapidly.

mistakes.w: Offspring from asexual reproduction are the same.
mistakes.r: Write that they are genetically identical (clones), so there is no variation in the population.

mistakes.w: Sexual reproduction makes the offspring stronger or better.
mistakes.r: It produces variation; if the environment changes, some individuals are likely to have characteristics that allow them to survive and reproduce. Not every offspring is better adapted.

mistakes.w: Asexual reproduction uses meiosis.
mistakes.r: Asexual reproduction uses mitosis only. Meiosis makes the gametes for sexual reproduction.

mistakes.w: No variation means the organisms will die.
mistakes.r: No variation is only a problem if the environment changes, for example a new disease: all individuals are equally susceptible, so the whole population could be killed.

mistakes.w: Sexual reproduction is a disadvantage because it needs two parents.
mistakes.r: State the consequence: a mate must be found, which takes time and energy, and an isolated individual cannot reproduce.

mistakes.w: Plants only reproduce asexually and animals only reproduce sexually.
mistakes.r: Many plants (for example strawberries) can do both, and most flowering plants reproduce sexually using pollen and ovules.

mistakes.w: Giving only one side when asked to compare.
mistakes.r: A comparison needs a statement about both types in each point, for example 'asexual offspring are genetically identical whereas sexual offspring are genetically different'.

exam.q: State the type of cell division that produces the offspring in asexual reproduction.
model: Mitosis.
exam.tip: Spell mitosis carefully; an ambiguous spelling between mitosis and meiosis is not credited.

exam.q: State one disadvantage of sexual reproduction.
model: A mate has to be found (which takes time and energy).
exam.tip: Use the specification wording: the requirement of finding a mate.

exam.q: Give two advantages of asexual reproduction.
model: There is no need to find a mate.
There is a rapid reproductive cycle, so many offspring are produced quickly.
exam.tip: Two marks, two different points. Both come straight from the specification.

exam.q: Explain why offspring produced by asexual reproduction are genetically identical.
model: There is only one parent, so no fusion of gametes and no mixing of genetic information.
The offspring are produced by mitosis, which makes exact copies of the chromosomes or DNA.
exam.tip: Mention both the single parent and mitosis.

exam.q: Strawberry plants can reproduce asexually using runners. Explain one advantage to the strawberry plant of reproducing in this way.
model: No mate (or pollination) is needed, or the reproductive cycle is rapid.
So many new plants are produced quickly, allowing the plant to colonise the area, or saving time and energy.
exam.tip: 'Explain' means a point plus a consequence.

exam.q: A farmer grows a field of potato plants that were all produced asexually from one parent plant. A new disease infects the field. Explain why the whole crop may be destroyed.
model: The plants are all genetically identical (clones).
So there is no variation in the population.
If one plant is susceptible to the disease, all are susceptible, so none have resistance and all may be killed.
exam.tip: Build a chain: identical -> no variation -> all equally affected.

exam.q: Explain why sexual reproduction is an advantage to a species when the environment changes.
model: Sexual reproduction produces variation in the population (offspring are genetically different).
Some individuals are likely to have characteristics that make them better adapted to the new conditions.
These individuals survive and reproduce, passing on their alleles, so the population does not die out.
exam.tip: Use the words variation, survive and reproduce.

exam.q: A species of animal lives at very low population density over a large area. Explain why reproducing only sexually could be a disadvantage for this species.
model: A mate must be found, which is difficult when individuals are far apart.
This takes a lot of time and energy, or some individuals may not find a mate and so produce no offspring.
exam.tip: Apply the idea of finding a mate to the context given.

exam.q: Compare the offspring produced by asexual reproduction with the offspring produced by sexual reproduction.
model: Offspring from asexual reproduction are genetically identical to the parent and to each other (clones).
Offspring from sexual reproduction are genetically different from each other and from both parents (show variation).
exam.tip: Each marking point is about one type; cover both.

exam.q: Some plants can reproduce both asexually and sexually. Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of asexual and sexual reproduction for these plants.
model: Asexual advantage: no need to find a mate or be pollinated, so time and energy are saved and one plant can colonise an area alone.
Asexual advantage: rapid reproductive cycle, so many offspring are produced quickly while conditions are favourable.
Asexual disadvantage: offspring are genetically identical, so there is no variation in the population.
So a change in the environment, such as a new disease, could affect or kill all of the plants.
Sexual advantage: offspring are genetically different, giving variation, so some are likely to survive a change and pass on their alleles.
Sexual disadvantage: a mate is required (pollen must be transferred), which takes time and energy and is slower, so fewer offspring are produced in a given time.
Conclusion: doing both gives rapid spread in stable conditions and variation as protection against change.
exam.tip: Level 3 needs both types, both advantages and disadvantages, with reasons linked together and a judgement.

worked.q: A bacterium reproduces asexually and, in ideal conditions, divides once every 20 minutes. Starting with one bacterium, calculate how many there will be after 3 hours and explain what this shows about asexual reproduction.
steps: Convert the time: 3 hours = 180 minutes.
Number of divisions = 180 / 20 = 9.
Each division doubles the number, so number of bacteria = 1 x 2^9.
Link to the spec: this shows the rapid reproductive cycle of asexual reproduction, with no mate needed, so the population increases very quickly.
worked.ans: 512 bacteria. Asexual reproduction has a rapid reproductive cycle and needs no mate, so numbers rise very quickly in favourable conditions.

worked.q: Aphids reproduce asexually in summer when there is plenty of food, and sexually in autumn. Explain the advantage of each method at these times. (4 marks)
steps: Summer (asexual): no mate is needed and the reproductive cycle is rapid.
Consequence: many offspring are produced quickly, so the population makes full use of the plentiful food.
Autumn (sexual): offspring are genetically different, so there is variation in the population.
Consequence: conditions are about to change, so some offspring are likely to have characteristics that let them survive, and the population continues.
worked.ans: Asexual reproduction in summer gives rapid population growth with no need for a mate while conditions are favourable; sexual reproduction in autumn gives variation, so some offspring are likely to survive the changing conditions.

worked.q: A banana crop consists of plants that are all clones. Evaluate the risk of growing a crop this way. (3 marks)
steps: Benefit: asexual reproduction means every plant has the same desired characteristics and new plants are produced quickly.
Risk: the plants are genetically identical, so there is no variation in the population.
Consequence: if a disease can infect one plant it can infect all of them, so the whole crop could be lost.
Judgement: the method is efficient in stable conditions but leaves the crop very vulnerable to a new disease.
worked.ans: Cloned crops are uniform and quick to produce, but with no variation a single disease could destroy every plant.

bio_edx.2.1.summary: Meiosis is the type of cell division that makes gametes (sex cells). One diploid cell divides to produce four daughter cells, each with half the number of chromosomes, so the gametes are haploid and genetically different from each other. Halving the chromosome number means that when two gametes fuse at fertilisation the normal diploid number is restored, and the genetic differences between gametes give variation in the offspring. Edexcel does not require the names of the stages of meiosis.

core.p: Spec point 3.3 asks you to **explain the role of meiotic cell division**, including the production of **four daughter cells**, each with **half the number of chromosomes**, and that this results in the formation of **genetically different haploid gametes**. The specification states that **the stages of meiosis are not required**.
bullets: You need the outcome (four, haploid, genetically different) and the reason it matters.
You do NOT need stage names such as prophase or anaphase for meiosis.
This point is examined in both Combined Science and separate Biology, at Foundation and Higher tier.
The three facts that score: **four** daughter cells, **half** the chromosome number (haploid), **genetically different**.

callouts.p: Meiosis produces four daughter cells, each with half the number of chromosomes, forming genetically different haploid gametes.

core.p: To understand meiosis you must be secure on chromosome numbers. Body cells contain chromosomes in **pairs**: one chromosome of each pair came from the mother and one from the father.
bullets: A **diploid** cell has **two sets** of chromosomes (written 2n). Body cells are diploid.
A **haploid** cell has **one set** of chromosomes (written n), which is half the diploid number. Gametes are haploid.
In humans the diploid number is **46** (23 pairs) and the haploid number is **23**.
The diploid number differs between species, but the haploid number is always half of it.
The two chromosomes in a pair carry the same genes but may carry different **alleles** (versions) of those genes.

callouts.p: Having one set of chromosomes: half the number found in a normal body cell.
Having two sets of chromosomes, one set from each parent.

core.h: What gametes are and where meiosis happens
core.p: **Gametes** are the sex cells that fuse at fertilisation. Meiosis happens only in the **reproductive organs**, in the cells that make gametes.
bullets: In animals the gametes are **sperm cells** (made in the testes) and **egg cells** (made in the ovaries).
In flowering plants the male gametes are in the **pollen** (made in the anthers) and the female gametes are egg cells in the **ovules** (in the ovary).
All other cell division in the body (growth, repair, replacing cells) is by mitosis, not meiosis.
The cell that starts meiosis is diploid; the gametes it produces are haploid.

callouts.p: A haploid sex cell (for example a sperm cell or an egg cell) that fuses with another gamete at fertilisation.

core.p: You do not need stage names, but you should be able to describe the overall sequence. The key idea is **one round of DNA replication followed by two divisions**.
bullets: **Before meiosis**, the cell's DNA **replicates**, so each chromosome is copied. Each chromosome now consists of two identical copies joined together.
**First division**: the chromosome pairs separate, one chromosome from each pair going to each of two new cells.
**Second division**: in each of those two cells the two copies of each chromosome are separated, so each divides again.
**Result**: **four** daughter cells.
Each daughter cell has only **one chromosome from each pair**, so it has **half the number of chromosomes**: it is **haploid**.
Each daughter cell has a **different combination of alleles**, so the four cells are **genetically different**.

callouts.p: DNA is replicated once but the cell divides twice. That is why the chromosome number is halved.

core.h: Why the gametes must be haploid
core.p: The first role of meiosis is to **halve the chromosome number**. This keeps the chromosome number constant from one generation to the next.
bullets: At **fertilisation**, a male gamete and a female gamete **fuse**, so their chromosomes are combined in one cell, the **zygote**.
Haploid + haploid = diploid. In humans: 23 + 23 = 46.
If gametes were diploid, the zygote would have double the normal number (46 + 46 = 92 in humans), and the number would **double every generation**.
Because gametes are haploid, the zygote has the **normal diploid number**, with one set of chromosomes from each parent.
The zygote then divides by **mitosis** to grow into an embryo, and every body cell made is diploid.

callouts.p: Gametes have half the number of chromosomes so that, when two gametes fuse at fertilisation, the zygote has the full (diploid) number of chromosomes.

core.h: Why the gametes are genetically different
core.p: The second role of meiosis is to produce **genetic variation**. No two gametes made by a person carry exactly the same combination of alleles.
bullets: Each gamete receives only **one chromosome from each pair**, and which one it receives (the one originally from the mother or the one from the father) is down to chance.
The pairs are sorted independently, so each gamete gets a **different mixture** of the mother's and father's chromosomes.
The two chromosomes of a pair can carry different alleles, so different mixtures of chromosomes mean **different combinations of alleles**.
Fertilisation is also random: any sperm can fuse with any egg, which increases variation further.
This is why brothers and sisters (other than identical twins) are genetically different even though they have the same parents.

callouts.p: Writing 'the cells are different' is too vague. The mark is for genetically different (or genetically varied) cells.

core.p: Genetically different gametes lead to genetically different offspring. Variation in a population is an advantage when conditions change.
bullets: Offspring produced by sexual reproduction are different from each other and from their parents.
If the environment changes, some individuals are more likely to have characteristics that let them survive.
Those individuals reproduce and pass on their alleles, so the species is more likely to survive.
So the two outcomes of meiosis link together: haploid cells make fertilisation possible, and genetic differences make the offspring varied.

core.p: Questions often ask you to compare the two types of cell division. Make sure each point of comparison says something about both.
bullets: Mitosis: growth, repair and asexual reproduction. Meiosis: production of gametes only.
Both begin with DNA replication.
The spelling matters: **meiosis** makes gam**e**tes; **mitosis** makes iden**t**ical cells.

callouts.p: Examiners do not credit a spelling that could be either word, such as 'meitosis' or 'miosis'. Learn both spellings exactly.

core.h: Chromosome numbers through the life cycle
core.p: Follow the chromosome number round a human life cycle to see how meiosis and fertilisation balance each other.
bullets: Diploid cells in the testes and ovaries (46) divide by **meiosis**.
This gives haploid gametes: sperm (23) and eggs (23).
**Fertilisation** joins the two: 23 + 23 = 46, a diploid zygote.
The zygote divides by **mitosis** many times, so all body cells are diploid (46).
Meiosis **halves** the number; fertilisation **restores** it.

callouts.p: Meiosis halves the chromosome number and fertilisation doubles it back, so the diploid number stays the same in every generation.

core.h: Working out chromosome numbers in questions
core.p: Exam questions often use an unfamiliar species and give either the diploid or the haploid number. The rule is always the same.
bullets: Haploid number = diploid number / 2.
Diploid number = haploid number x 2.
Gametes (sperm, egg, pollen grain nucleus) are haploid; all other cells mentioned (skin, muscle, leaf, zygote, embryo) are diploid.
Number of gametes made = number of cells undergoing meiosis x 4.
Example: a dog body cell has 78 chromosomes, so a dog sperm cell has 39.

callouts.p: Before calculating, decide whether the cell named is a gamete (haploid) or a body cell or zygote (diploid).

core.h: Putting it together: the role of meiosis
core.p: When a question asks you to **explain the role of meiosis**, give the outcome and the reason for each feature.
bullets: Meiosis produces **gametes** for sexual reproduction.
It produces **four** daughter cells from one parent cell.
Each has **half the number of chromosomes** (haploid), so that the diploid number is restored at fertilisation.
The gametes are **genetically different**, which causes variation in the offspring.

analogy.t: Dealing from two packs of cards
analogy.p: Imagine a body cell holds two packs of cards, a red-backed pack from mum and a blue-backed pack from dad: two of every card. Meiosis first photocopies everything, then deals the cards out over two rounds into **four hands**, so that each hand ends up with exactly **one of every card** (one full set, haploid) but a random mixture of red-backed and blue-backed cards. Every hand is a complete set, yet no two hands have the same mix of colours, just as gametes are genetically different. At fertilisation two hands, one from each parent, are put together to make two full packs again. Where it breaks down: real chromosomes are not dealt by a dealer but are pulled apart inside the cell, and two cards of the same value from different packs are identical, whereas paired chromosomes can carry different alleles.

Cell division that produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells, used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction.
A haploid sex cell, such as a sperm cell or an egg cell.
Having one set of chromosomes, half the number in a body cell (23 in humans).
Having two sets of chromosomes, one from each parent (46 in humans).
A long molecule of DNA, found in the nucleus, that carries genes.
The new cells produced when a parent cell divides.
The fusion of a male gamete and a female gamete to form a zygote.
The diploid cell formed by the fusion of two haploid gametes.
The copying of a cell's DNA, which happens once before meiosis begins.
A different version of the same gene.
Having different combinations of alleles; true of the four cells produced by meiosis.
Differences between individuals of the same species.
The male gamete in animals; haploid.
The female gamete; haploid.

mistakes.w: Meiosis produces two cells.
mistakes.r: Meiosis produces four daughter cells; it is mitosis that produces two.

mistakes.w: The cells made by meiosis are different.
mistakes.r: They are genetically different (each has a different combination of alleles).

mistakes.w: Gametes have half the DNA so they are smaller.
mistakes.r: Gametes have half the number of chromosomes (haploid) so that the diploid number is restored when two gametes fuse at fertilisation.

mistakes.w: Human gametes have 46 chromosomes.
mistakes.r: Human gametes are haploid and have 23 chromosomes; body cells have 46.

mistakes.w: Meiosis is used for growth and repair.
mistakes.r: Mitosis is used for growth and repair. Meiosis only produces gametes.

mistakes.w: The DNA replicates twice in meiosis because there are two divisions.
mistakes.r: The DNA replicates only once, before the first division, and the cell then divides twice.

mistakes.w: Spelling it 'meitosis' or 'miosis'.
mistakes.r: It must be clearly spelt meiosis; ambiguous spellings are not credited.

mistakes.w: The zygote is haploid.
mistakes.r: The zygote is diploid because it is formed from the fusion of two haploid gametes.

exam.q: State the name of the type of cell division that produces gametes.
model: Meiosis.
exam.tip: Correct spelling is essential.

exam.q: State how many daughter cells are produced when one cell divides by meiosis.
model: Four.
exam.tip: Two is the answer for mitosis.

exam.q: A human body cell contains 46 chromosomes. State the number of chromosomes in a human sperm cell.
exam.tip: Gametes are haploid: halve the diploid number.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term haploid.
model: Having one set of chromosomes, or half the number of chromosomes of a body cell.
exam.tip: Refer to chromosomes, not just 'half the DNA'.

exam.q: Describe the cells produced by meiosis.
model: Four daughter cells are produced.
They are haploid, with half the number of chromosomes of the parent cell.
They are genetically different from each other.
exam.tip: Three marks: four, haploid, genetically different.

exam.q: Explain why gametes must have half the number of chromosomes found in body cells.
model: At fertilisation two gametes fuse, combining their chromosomes.
So the zygote has the full (diploid) number of chromosomes, and the number does not double each generation.
exam.tip: Mention fertilisation and the diploid number.

exam.q: Give two differences between the daughter cells produced by mitosis and those produced by meiosis.
model: Mitosis produces two daughter cells whereas meiosis produces four.
Mitosis produces diploid, genetically identical cells whereas meiosis produces haploid, genetically different cells.
exam.tip: Each difference must mention both types of division.

exam.q: A horse has 64 chromosomes in each body cell. State the number of chromosomes in a horse egg cell and in a horse zygote.
model: Egg cell: 32.
Zygote: 64.
exam.tip: Egg is haploid (64 / 2); the zygote is diploid again (32 + 32).

exam.q: Explain how meiosis leads to variation in the offspring produced by sexual reproduction.
model: Meiosis produces gametes that are genetically different from each other.
Each gamete contains a different combination of alleles (a different mixture of the chromosomes that came from the mother and the father).
Any male gamete can fuse with any female gamete at fertilisation, so each offspring has a different combination of alleles.
exam.tip: Link gametes -> fertilisation -> offspring.

exam.q: Explain the role of meiosis in sexual reproduction.
model: Meiosis produces gametes (sperm and egg cells).
One cell divides to form four daughter cells.
Each daughter cell is haploid, with half the number of chromosomes, so that fertilisation restores the diploid number.
The gametes are genetically different, which causes variation in the offspring.
exam.tip: Outcome plus reason for each feature.

exam.q: Compare mitosis and meiosis. Your answer should include the products of each type of division and their roles in organisms.
model: Mitosis involves one division; meiosis involves two divisions.
Mitosis produces two daughter cells; meiosis produces four.
Mitosis daughter cells are diploid, with the same chromosome number as the parent cell; meiosis daughter cells are haploid, with half the number.
Mitosis daughter cells are genetically identical; meiosis daughter cells are genetically different.
Mitosis is used for growth, repair and asexual reproduction; meiosis is used to produce gametes for sexual reproduction.
In both, the DNA is replicated once before division begins.
Haploid gametes allow the diploid number to be restored at fertilisation, and genetic differences give variation.
exam.tip: Organise the answer feature by feature, giving both types each time, and include similarities as well as differences.

worked.q: A cat body cell contains 38 chromosomes. (a) How many chromosomes are in a cat sperm cell? (b) How many are in the zygote formed at fertilisation? (c) 150 cells in a cat's testis each complete meiosis. How many sperm cells could be produced?
steps: (a) A sperm cell is a gamete, so it is haploid: 38 / 2 = 19.
(b) The zygote is formed when a sperm (19) fuses with an egg (19): 19 + 19 = 38.
(c) Each cell that undergoes meiosis produces four daughter cells: 150 x 4 = 600.

worked.q: Explain why two children with the same parents (who are not identical twins) are genetically different. (3 marks)
steps: Start with meiosis: each parent's gametes are produced by meiosis, which makes genetically different haploid cells.
Give the reason: each gamete has a different combination of alleles.
Add fertilisation: each child came from a different sperm fusing with a different egg, so each has a different combination of alleles.
worked.ans: Meiosis makes every gamete genetically different, and each child develops from a different pair of gametes fusing at fertilisation, so each child inherits a different combination of alleles.

worked.q: A student writes: 'Meiosis makes two identical cells for growth.' Correct each error in this statement.
steps: Number: meiosis makes four daughter cells, not two.
Genetics: the cells are genetically different, not identical.
Chromosome number: add that they are haploid (half the number of chromosomes).
Purpose: meiosis produces gametes for sexual reproduction; growth uses mitosis.
worked.ans: Meiosis makes four genetically different haploid cells (gametes) for sexual reproduction. The student has described mitosis.

bio_edx.2.2.summary: DNA is a polymer made of repeating units called nucleotides, each consisting of a sugar, a phosphate group and one of four bases (A, T, C or G) attached to the sugar. Two strands of nucleotides are linked by complementary base pairs (A with T, C with G) joined by weak hydrogen bonds, and the two strands coil to form a double helix. The genome is the entire DNA of an organism, and a gene is a section of a DNA molecule that codes for a specific protein.

core.p: Spec point 3.4 asks you to **describe DNA as a polymer** made up of (a) two strands coiled to form a **double helix**, (b) strands linked by a series of **complementary base pairs** joined together by **weak hydrogen bonds**, and (c) **nucleotides** that consist of a **sugar and phosphate group with one of the four different bases attached to the sugar**. Spec point 3.5 asks you to describe the **genome** as the entire DNA of an organism and a **gene** as a section of a DNA molecule that codes for a specific protein.
bullets: Examined in both Combined Science and separate Biology, at Foundation and Higher tier.
Most marks come from precise wording: polymer, nucleotide, sugar, phosphate, base, complementary, hydrogen bonds, double helix.
The two definitions (genome and gene) are regularly asked as 1-mark and 2-mark questions.
How the base sequence is used to make a protein belongs to a different spec point; here you only need the structure and the two definitions.

callouts.p: The entire DNA of an organism.
A section of a DNA molecule that codes for a specific protein.

core.p: DNA is a very long molecule. It is a **polymer**: a large molecule made by joining many similar small units (**monomers**) together in a chain. The monomers of DNA are **nucleotides**.
bullets: Polymer = many repeating units joined together.
The repeating unit (monomer) of DNA is the **nucleotide**.
A single DNA molecule contains a huge number of nucleotides joined in two long strands.
There are only **four different nucleotides**, which differ only in the base they contain.
The **order** of the nucleotides (and so of the bases) along the strand is what carries the genetic information.

callouts.p: Nucleotide = monomer. DNA = polymer made of many nucleotides.

core.p: Each nucleotide is made of **three parts**. The spec wording is exact: a nucleotide consists of a **sugar and phosphate group with one of the four different bases attached to the sugar**.
bullets: A **sugar** (the sugar in DNA is deoxyribose, but 'sugar' is enough at GCSE).
A **phosphate group**, attached to the sugar.
A **base**, also attached to the **sugar** (not to the phosphate).
So the sugar sits in the middle, joined to both the phosphate group and the base.
In diagrams the phosphate is usually drawn as a circle, the sugar as a pentagon and the base as a rectangle or shaped block.

callouts.p: The base is attached to the sugar. Drawing or describing the base joined to the phosphate group is a common error.

core.p: There are **four different bases** in DNA. They are usually written as single letters, but you should know the full names too.
bullets: **A** = adenine
**T** = thymine
**C** = cytosine
**G** = guanine
The four nucleotides are identical apart from the base, so the base is what makes one nucleotide different from another.
The sequence of bases along a strand is the genetic code.

callouts.p: Write thymine, not thiamine (a vitamin), and adenine, not adenosine. Letters alone are usually accepted, but learn the names.

core.p: Nucleotides join together in a long chain to form a **strand**. The sugar of one nucleotide is joined to the phosphate group of the next, forming a chain of alternating sugars and phosphates.
bullets: This alternating chain is called the **sugar-phosphate backbone**.
The backbone is the same all the way along every DNA molecule; it gives the strand its strength.
The **bases stick out** from the sugars on one side of the backbone, pointing towards the other strand.
In the ladder model of DNA, the two backbones are the **sides** of the ladder and the paired bases are the **rungs**.

core.p: A DNA molecule has **two strands**. The strands are linked because each base on one strand pairs with a particular base on the other strand. The pairing is always the same and is called **complementary base pairing**.
bullets: **A always pairs with T.**
**C always pairs with G.**
The bases have shapes that fit only their partner, which is why A never pairs with C or G.
Because of this rule, if you know the sequence of bases on one strand you can work out the sequence on the other strand.
Example: one strand reads A T G C C A; the complementary strand reads T A C G G T.
It also means the **amount of A equals the amount of T**, and the **amount of C equals the amount of G**, in any double-stranded DNA molecule.

callouts.p: A with T, C with G. Memory aid: the straight-line letters (A, T) pair together and the curved letters (C, G) pair together.
Pairs of bases that always bond with each other in DNA: A with T and C with G.

core.p: The two bases in each complementary pair are joined together by **weak hydrogen bonds**. These bonds hold the two strands of the DNA molecule together.
bullets: Hydrogen bonds form **between the bases** of opposite strands, not between the sugars and phosphates.
Each individual hydrogen bond is **weak**, but there are so many along the molecule that together they hold the two strands firmly.

Because the bonds are weak, the two strands can be **separated** when the cell needs to, without breaking the strands themselves. This is how the DNA can be copied and how the code in a gene can be read.
The bonds within each strand (along the sugar-phosphate backbone) are much stronger, so the order of bases in each strand is kept intact.

callouts.p: The mark is for 'hydrogen bonds' (weak hydrogen bonds). Writing only 'bonds' or 'the bases stick together' does not score.

core.p: The two linked strands are not flat like a ladder. They are **coiled** (twisted) around each other to form a spiral shape called a **double helix**.
bullets: **Double** = two strands. **Helix** = a spiral or coil.
Imagine a ladder twisted along its length: the sides are the two sugar-phosphate backbones and the rungs are the complementary base pairs.
The bases are on the **inside** of the helix and the sugar-phosphate backbones are on the **outside**.
The correct description is 'two strands coiled to form a double helix'. A single strand is not a double helix.

callouts.t: Describing DNA structure for 3 or 4 marks
callouts.p: Give: two strands; coiled into a double helix; made of nucleotides (sugar, phosphate group, base); strands linked by complementary base pairs (A-T, C-G); joined by weak hydrogen bonds.

core.p: The **genome** is the **entire DNA of an organism**. It includes every gene and also all the DNA between the genes that does not code for proteins.
bullets: Almost every body cell of an organism contains a complete copy of the genome.
In animal and plant cells, most of the DNA is in the **nucleus**, organised into **chromosomes**.
Each chromosome contains one very long, coiled DNA molecule carrying many genes.
Different species have different genomes, and individuals of the same species have slightly different genomes.
Do not define the genome as 'all the genes': genes are only part of the DNA. The definition is **all (the entire) DNA**.

callouts.p: The Edexcel definition is the entire DNA of an organism. Much of the genome does not code for proteins.

core.p: A **gene** is a **section of a DNA molecule that codes for a specific protein**. Each chromosome carries many genes along its length.
bullets: A gene is a particular **sequence of bases** on the DNA.
The order of bases in a gene determines which protein is made, so different genes code for different proteins.
Proteins (such as enzymes, hormones and structural proteins) control how cells work and so determine the organism's characteristics.
A gene is much shorter than the whole DNA molecule: one DNA molecule contains many genes.
Size order, largest to smallest: genome, chromosome, gene, nucleotide (base).

core.h: Using the pairing rule in calculations
core.p: Because A always pairs with T and C always pairs with G, the numbers (or percentages) of paired bases are equal. This lets you calculate the proportions of all four bases from just one.
bullets: Number of A = number of T; number of C = number of G.
A + T + C + G = 100% of the bases.
If you know the percentage of one base, its partner has the same percentage; the remainder is shared equally between the other two.
Example: 30% A means 30% T; that leaves 40%, so 20% C and 20% G.
The same idea works with numbers of bases rather than percentages.

analogy.p: Think of DNA as a very long **zip that has been twisted into a spiral**. The two fabric tapes down the sides are the two sugar-phosphate backbones; the teeth are the bases. Each tooth only locks with its partner on the opposite side, like A with T and C with G, and the grip between teeth is weak enough for the zip to be undone and done up again, like hydrogen bonds letting the strands separate, while the tapes themselves stay intact. Twist the closed zip and you have a double helix. Where it breaks down: zip teeth are all the same, whereas DNA has four different bases whose order carries information; and a real zip is not coiled.

exam.q: State what is meant by the term genome.
model: The entire DNA of an organism.
exam.tip: 'All the genes' is not the Edexcel definition.

exam.q: Name the bonds that hold the two strands of a DNA molecule together.
model: (Weak) hydrogen bonds.
exam.tip: The word hydrogen is required.

exam.q: State the name given to the shape of a DNA molecule.
model: Double helix.
exam.tip: Both words are needed.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by the term gene.
model: A section (length) of a DNA molecule.
That codes for a specific protein.
exam.tip: Two marks, two ideas: what it is and what it does.

exam.q: Name the three components of a DNA nucleotide.
model: Sugar and phosphate (group).
Base.
exam.tip: All three parts are needed for full marks; a named base such as adenine is acceptable for 'base'.

exam.q: One strand of a DNA molecule has the base sequence T A C G G A T. Give the base sequence of the complementary strand.
model: A T G C C T A.
exam.tip: Work along one base at a time: A pairs with T, C pairs with G.

exam.q: Explain why DNA is described as a polymer.
model: It is a long molecule made of many repeating units (monomers) joined together.
The repeating units are nucleotides.
exam.tip: Name the monomer.

exam.q: In a sample of DNA, 22% of the bases are guanine. Calculate the percentage of the bases that are adenine.
model: Guanine pairs with cytosine, so cytosine = 22%; G + C = 44%.
exam.tip: Show the working; one mark is usually available for finding the partner base total.

exam.q: Explain how the two strands of a DNA molecule are held together.
model: Bases on one strand pair with bases on the other strand (complementary base pairing).
A pairs with T and C pairs with G.
The base pairs are joined by weak hydrogen bonds.
exam.tip: Pairing, the rule, then the bond type.

exam.q: Describe the structure of a DNA molecule.
model: It is made of two strands coiled to form a double helix.
Each strand is a polymer of nucleotides, each made of a sugar, a phosphate group and a base.
There are four bases (A, T, C and G), each attached to a sugar, and the sugars and phosphates form the backbone of each strand.
The strands are linked by complementary base pairs (A with T, C with G) joined by weak hydrogen bonds.
exam.tip: Work from the overall shape down to the nucleotide, or the other way round, so nothing is missed.

exam.q: A student says: 'A gene, a chromosome and the genome are all the same thing because they are all made of DNA.' Discuss this statement, describing how these terms are related and how the structure of DNA allows it to carry a code.
model: All three are made of DNA, but they are different amounts of DNA.
The genome is the entire DNA of an organism.
A chromosome is one long, coiled DNA molecule; the genome is made up of all the chromosomes.
A gene is a short section of a DNA molecule that codes for a specific protein; each chromosome carries many genes.
DNA is a polymer of nucleotides, each with a sugar, a phosphate group and one of four bases (A, T, C, G).
The order (sequence) of bases along the DNA is the code; different genes have different base sequences and so code for different proteins.
The two strands are linked by complementary base pairs (A-T, C-G) with weak hydrogen bonds and coiled into a double helix.
exam.tip: Define each term, show the size relationship, then link structure to the idea of a base sequence.

worked.q: In a DNA molecule, 18% of the bases are thymine (T). Calculate the percentage of each of the other three bases.
steps: T pairs with A, so the percentage of A equals the percentage of T: A = 18%.
The rest must be C and G: 100 - 36 = 64%.
C pairs with G, so they are equal: 64 / 2 = 32% each.

worked.q: A section of one DNA strand has the sequence G G A T C C A T. (a) Write the sequence of the complementary strand. (b) How many hydrogen-bonded base pairs are there in this section? (c) How many nucleotides are there in this double-stranded section?
steps: (a) Apply the pairing rule to each base in turn: G-C, G-C, A-T, T-A, C-G, C-G, A-T, T-A.
So the complementary strand reads C C T A G G T A.
(b) Each base on the strand forms one pair with a base on the other strand: 8 bases gives 8 base pairs.
(c) Each strand has 8 nucleotides and there are two strands: 8 x 2 = 16 nucleotides.
worked.ans: (a) C C T A G G T A (b) 8 base pairs (c) 16 nucleotides

worked.q: A length of DNA contains 1200 bases in total. 240 of them are cytosine. Calculate the number of adenine bases.
steps: C pairs with G, so G = 240.
A pairs with T, so A = T = 720 / 2 = 360.
